title: A parity plot asks whether predictions fall on the diagonal, and the test points, not the training points, answer it
summary: A parity plot puts prediction against truth. Training points on the diagonal only show that the model can reproduce what it was given. Here the training points lie exactly on the line while the held-out test points form a flat cloud, and a small percentage error is partly an artefact of how narrow the response range is.

media.alt: Square parity plot of predicted eta against actual eta, both axes from about 5.37 to 5.70. A red dashed diagonal is labelled perfect fit. Blue open circles for training points lie exactly on the diagonal. Black filled dots for test points scatter horizontally between about 5.50 and 5.57 on the vertical axis for actual values from 5.39 to 5.69. The title reads Hybrid PRS v2, ridge polynomial degree 2 plus Gaussian process, max relative error train 0.00 percent, test 3.05 percent.

source.caption: Gaussian-process surrogate parity plot
source.note: Single-figure group. The page describes the plot as a surrogate fit to methyl-butanoate data; the response eta is not defined on the figure. Read as drawn, the test points do not follow the diagonal.
group: 07_parity_v2_GP: Gaussian-process surrogate parity plot (the only figure in this group)

read_the_figure.question: Does the surrogate predict values it has not seen as well as values it was fitted to?
read_the_figure.axes: x: actual value of the response, eta, from the simulation, about 5.37 to 5.70. y: the model's predicted eta on the same scale. The red dashed line is y = x, the perfect fit. Blue open circles are the training points; black dots are the held-out test points.
look_at: Training points (blue) all sit on the red line, and the title says train max relative error is 0.00 percent: the model has reproduced its training data exactly, as an interpolating model such as a Gaussian process can.
Test points (black) do not follow the line. Their predictions stay between about 5.50 and 5.57 whatever the actual value, which runs from about 5.39 to 5.69. The cloud is flat, not diagonal.

The title reports a test maximum relative error of 3.05 percent. Compare that with the width of the actual range: it is about 5 percent of the mean. A model that predicted the mean for every point would score nearly the same maximum error.
Axes are linear with equal range on both sides, so a perfect model would sit on the 45 degree line.
read_the_figure.proves: Only that the model reproduces its training data. For generalisation, the test cloud is the evidence, and here it shows little or no predictive skill beyond the mean of the response.
if_wrong: A test cloud that is flat or very much narrower than the actual range means the model outputs nearly the same value for every input: it has not learned the dependence, or the inputs carry little information about the response.
Training exactly on the line together with a poor test cloud is the classic sign of an interpolating model that over-fits.
A single summary percentage hides all of this: always show the test scatter.
must_check: Test data are truly held out: no test point is also in the training set.
Axes have equal scale and range; the perfect-fit line is drawn.
Error is reported in a form that includes a baseline (for example against predicting the mean), or the response range is stated.
The number of train and test points is given: it is not printed here.
The response eta and its units are defined: they are not defined here.
as_drawn: Actual range read by eye: about 5.39 to 5.69 for the test points. Predicted test range: about 5.50 to 5.57.
The predictions' spread is therefore roughly 0.07 against an actual spread of about 0.30: about a quarter.

A constant prediction at the middle of the test range, about 5.54, would have a maximum relative error of about (5.69 - 5.54) / 5.54, about 2.7 percent, or 2.8 percent at the low end: of the same size as the 3.05 percent printed in the title.

terms.meaning: A scatter of predicted against actual values with the line y = x drawn. Points on the line are perfect predictions.
Training points are used to fit the model. Test points are held back and used only to judge it.
A cheap model, such as a polynomial or a Gaussian process, fitted to a few runs of an expensive simulation so that it can be evaluated many times.
A flexible regression model that interpolates the training data and gives a prediction and an uncertainty everywhere. Its smoothness is set by a kernel (here Matern 5/2).
A polynomial regression with a penalty on large coefficients, which keeps a high-degree fit stable.
The largest value of |prediction - actual| / |actual| over a set of points. It is a worst-case measure and depends on the size of the response.
Fitting the training data (including its noise) so closely that predictions on new data are worse than a simpler model's.
The simplest possible predictor, usually the mean of the training responses. A model is useful only if it beats it on test data.

remember: Training performance is not evidence of predictive power; only held-out data are.
An interpolating model such as a GP without noise passes through the training points by construction, so a perfect training fit is expected and uninformative.
A relative error means little without the spread of the response: a narrow response range makes any constant look accurate.
R-squared on test data compares the model with the mean predictor; a value near 0 means no skill.
Always plot the test scatter next to the single number.

understand.title: Why the blue points are on the line
understand.text: A Gaussian process with a tiny noise term is built to pass through every training point. So the training error is 0.00 percent by construction. It tells you the arithmetic works, not that the model is good.

understand.title: What the flat black cloud says
understand.text: If the model had learned how eta depends on its inputs, test predictions would rise with the actual value. Here they hardly move: the model returns close to the average for any new input. That is what a GP does when its inputs are far from the training points in the kernel's length scales, or when the response depends little on the inputs it was given.

understand.title: Why 3.05 percent looks fine and is not
understand.text: The response lies between about 5.4 and 5.7, a total spread of about 5 percent of its mean. Any prediction near the mean is therefore within about 3 percent of every actual value. A small relative error here is a property of the data, not of the model.

steps.title: The error measure
steps.note: The title's 'max rel err' is a worst-case relative error over the set. It depends on both the model and the spread of y.

steps.title: The baseline error of a constant
steps.note: If you always predict the mean, the worst relative error is about the largest distance from the mean over the mean. For a response between 5.39 and 5.69 around 5.54 that is about 2.7 percent, computed from values read off the plot.

steps.title: Skill relative to the mean
steps.note: R-squared on the test set. Equal to 1 for a perfect model, 0 for the mean predictor, negative if the model is worse than the mean. A flat cloud on a parity plot gives a value near 0.

steps.title: GP interpolation
steps.note: With noise sigma_n squared near zero, the prediction equals y at every training input. Far from all training inputs the kernel vector k_* goes to zero and the prediction reverts to the prior mean.

steps.title: Where the Matern kernel loses its grip
steps.note: The Matern 5/2 kernel falls with distance r over the length scale l. With ARD there is one l per input; an input with a very long l is ignored, and one with a very short l makes predictions revert to the mean away from the data.

steps.title: A leave-out test is the honest estimate
steps.note: The error is averaged over points that played no role in the fit. The same quantity on training points is optimistic.

worked.title: Is 3.05 percent good for this response?
worked.problem: The test responses run from about 5.39 to 5.69, and a model that predicts a constant 5.54 would have worst errors at the two ends. Compare the constant's worst error with the printed 3.05 percent.

solution.text: Distance of the high end from the constant, divided by the value at the high end.
Distance of the low end from the constant, divided by the value at the low end.

worked.answer: A constant prediction gets a worst error of about 2.6 to 2.8 percent, comparable to the 3.05 percent printed. So the number does not show skill: the test scatter does the real work, and it is flat.

analyze.q: Give two different reasons a model can have a perfect training fit and a flat test cloud, and one experiment for each.
analyze.hint: Over-fitting with too flexible a model; inputs that do not explain the response; test points outside the training range.

analyze.q: The title reports the maximum, not the mean, relative error. How would the picture change if the mean were reported?
analyze.hint: The mean is smaller than the max for any scatter.

evaluate.q: Would you use this surrogate in place of the simulation on the strength of this figure? What is the minimum extra evidence?
evaluate.hint: R-squared on test data, a baseline, the number of points, and a cross-validation.

evaluate.q: Is the format of the figure fair? State what is good and what is missing.
evaluate.hint: Good: held-out points distinguished, line drawn, equal axes. Missing: counts, R-squared, definition of eta.

create: Redraw the parity plot with the baseline (mean predictor) as a horizontal line and test R-squared in the title.
Design a cross-validation study that would tell you whether the inputs carry enough information to predict eta at all.

checks.q: Why do training points sit exactly on the diagonal for a Gaussian process?
checks.hint: What does the posterior mean do at a training input when noise is zero?
checks.answer: With negligible noise the GP is an interpolator: its mean passes through every training observation, so training error is zero by construction.

checks.q: A response runs from 10.0 to 10.6, and a model predicts 10.3 for every point. What is its worst relative error?
checks.hint: Largest distance from 10.3 over the value there.
checks.answer: At the low end: 0.3 / 10.0 = 3.0 percent. At the high end: 0.3 / 10.6 = 2.8 percent. The worst is 3.0 percent.

checks.q: What does a horizontal band of test points on a parity plot tell you?
checks.hint: The prediction does not depend on the actual value.
checks.answer: The model's output does not vary with the truth: it predicts roughly the mean regardless. It has no predictive skill beyond the mean.

checks.q: Someone says: 'train error 0.00 percent, test error 3.05 percent, so the model generalises well'. Respond.
checks.answer: The 3.05 percent is about the error of predicting the mean, because the response range is narrow. The test scatter is flat. So the numbers do not show generalisation; they show a narrow response.

checks.q: What single number would you add to the title to make the claim honest?
checks.hint: It should compare the model with the mean predictor.
checks.answer: Test R-squared (or the ratio of the model's test RMSE to the standard deviation of the test responses). Near 0 means no skill.
